clinicalPearls: Caused mainly by heterozygous variants in COL5A1 or COL5A2 affecting type V collagen, with rare specific COL1A1 arginine-to-cysteine substitutions; autosomal dominant.
Hallmark combination of marked skin hyperextensibility, atrophic (papyraceous, cigarette-paper) scarring and generalised joint hypermobility.
Skin is soft and doughy and splits easily over bony prominences such as knees, elbows, shins and forehead, leaving gaping wounds.
Wound healing is delayed with wide atrophic scars and a strong tendency to suture dehiscence, making surgery challenging.
Easy bruising, molluscoid pseudotumours over scars and calcified subcutaneous spheroids are common minor features.
Joint hypermobility leads to recurrent subluxation and dislocation, sprains, chronic pain and early osteoarthritis.
Aortic root dilatation may occur but is usually mild and non-progressive; baseline echocardiography is advised.
Major arterial rupture is not a typical feature and its presence should prompt reconsideration of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
reference.pathophysiology: Type V collagen is a quantitatively minor fibrillar collagen that co-assembles with type I collagen and regulates the nucleation and diameter of collagen fibrils in skin, tendon and other tissues. Most patients carry a heterozygous COL5A1 variant causing haploinsufficiency, or a structural COL5A1 or COL5A2 variant, that reduces or distorts functional type V collagen. The resulting dysregulated fibrillogenesis produces enlarged, irregular composite fibrils, described as collagen cauliflowers or flowers on electron microscopy, which weaken the dermis and other connective tissues. This impairs tensile strength and wound repair and loosens ligamentous support, accounting for the fragile hyperextensible skin, poor scarring and joint instability.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment with Beighton hypermobility scoring and skin examination
Molecular genetic testing of COL5A1 and COL5A2, with COL1A1 where indicated
Skin biopsy for electron microscopy showing irregular collagen fibrils
Baseline echocardiography to assess the aortic root
Assessment and genetic counselling of first-degree relatives
Dermal fibroblast studies where the molecular diagnosis is unclear
redFlags: Significant or progressive aortic root dilatation
Major wound dehiscence or non-healing surgical wounds
An arterial rupture or dissection suggesting reclassification as vascular EDS
Obstetric complications such as tissue tearing or prolapse
Rapidly enlarging haematoma after minor trauma
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal in most patients. Morbidity arises from skin fragility, recurrent joint instability, chronic pain and the cosmetic and functional burden of poor wound healing.
pitfalls: Confusing classical EDS with hypermobile EDS, which has no confirmatory molecular test, leading to diagnostic imprecision.
Attributing all generalised hypermobility to classical EDS without the characteristic skin and scarring features.
Using high-tension suturing rather than tension-free, layered closure, worsening scar dehiscence.
Failing to arrange baseline cardiac imaging or to counsel relatives about inheritance.
management: Protection of fragile skin through avoidance of trauma, protective padding over bony prominences and meticulous low-tension wound closure with deep, long-retained sutures
Joint stabilisation with physiotherapy to strengthen periarticular muscles, low-impact exercise and bracing or orthoses to reduce subluxation and dislocation
Chronic pain management with physiotherapy and appropriate analgesia
Baseline and periodic echocardiography to assess the aortic root
Preoperative counselling of surgical and anaesthetic teams about tissue fragility and delayed wound healing
Coordinated multidisciplinary care through clinical genetics, dermatology, physiotherapy and rheumatology
Genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant type V collagen disorder with assessment of first-degree relatives
